title: Sorting
html:
Sorting arranges data in increasing or decreasing order. It is the most studied problem in computer science because so much else — binary search, deduplication, merging, finding medians, grouping — becomes easy once the data is sorted. These notes cover the library sorts you should actually call and the classic algorithms you must be able to write and analyse: bubble, selection, insertion, merge, quick and heap sort.

Sorting — rearranging a sequence so that every element is ≤ the one after it (ascending) or ≥ it (descending), according to a comparison — numeric, alphabetic, or any custom key.

Comparison of sorting algorithms

The two properties interviewers ask about after time complexity are stability (equal elements keep their original relative order) and whether the sort is in-place (needs only O(1) — or O(log n) stack — extra memory).

AlgorithmBestAverageWorstExtra spaceStableIn-placeNotes
Bubble sortO(n)*O(n²)O(n²)O(1)yesyes*with the swapped flag; academic only
Selection sortO(n²)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)noyesfewest writes: at most n − 1 swaps
Insertion sortO(n)O(n²)O(n²)O(1)yesyesbest for small or nearly sorted input; used inside Timsort / introsort
Merge sortO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(n)yesnolinked lists and external sorting; guaranteed n log n
Quick sortO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n²)O(log n) stacknoyesfastest in practice: cache-friendly, low constants
Heap sortO(n log n)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(1)noyesguaranteed n log n in place; poor cache behaviour
Timsort (library)O(n)O(n log n)O(n log n)O(n)yesnomerge sort + insertion sort on natural runs; Python, Java objects, V8
Key point

Any sort that only compares elements needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case — there are n! orderings and each comparison rules out at most half. Merge, heap and quick sort are optimal in that sense; counting and radix sort beat it only by not comparing (they index on the values).

Built-in sorting in each language

In real code you call the library sort. Know what it runs, whether it is stable, and how to pass a key or comparator.

LanguageCallAlgorithmStableCustom order
Pythonsorted(iterable, key=, reverse=) → new list · list.sort() in placeTimsortyeskey= function (len, abs, lambda p: (p.x, p.y))
C++std::sort(begin, end, cmp)introsort (quick + heap + insertion)nocomparator: greater<int>(), lambda
C++std::stable_sort(begin, end, cmp)merge sortyessame comparator
JavaArrays.sort(int[]) (primitives)dual-pivot quicksortn/a (primitives are indistinguishable)—
JavaArrays.sort(T[]), Collections.sort(list), list.sort(cmp)TimsortyesComparator.comparingInt(...), reverseOrder()
JavaScriptarr.sort(cmp) in place · arr.toSorted(cmp) copyTimsort (V8)yes (since ES2019)(a, b) => a - b — required for numbers
Pitfall

JavaScript's arr.sort() without a comparator converts every element to a string and compares the strings. Numbers come out in dictionary order — a classic bug.

Python: sort() and sorted()

list.sort()sorted(iterable)
Works onlists onlyany iterable: list, tuple, string, set, dict (its keys), generator
Resultsorts in place, returns Nonereturns a new list; the input is untouched
Parameterskey=, reverse=key=, reverse= — identical meaning
AlgorithmTimsort, stable, O(n log n) worst, O(n) on sorted inputsame
Pitfall

x = l.sort() leaves x as None. Use l.sort() on its own line, or x = sorted(l).

Sorting objects. Either pass a key function that extracts the field to compare, or define __lt__ on the class so the objects compare themselves. A tuple key such as (p.x, p.y) sorts by x and breaks ties by y.

sorted() on other iterables — the result is always a list, even for a tuple, string or set. A dict sorts by its keys.

Key point

Timsort (Tim Peters, 2002) is a hybrid: it finds already-ordered runs in the input, sorts short runs with insertion sort, then merges runs with merge sort. That is why it is stable, O(n log n) in the worst case and O(n) on already-sorted data. Java uses it for objects and V8 for Array.prototype.sort.

Stability

Stable sort — a sort that keeps elements with equal keys in the same relative order they had in the input.

Why it matters: stability lets you sort by several fields in passes. Sort by the secondary key first, then stably by the primary key — rows with the same primary key stay in secondary order. Spreadsheets, SQL ORDER BY a, b and "sort by marks, then alphabetically" all rely on this. It is also what makes sort by marks leave an already alphabetical list alphabetical within each group.

StableNot stableWhy
Bubble sortSelection sortselection swaps the minimum over elements it has not compared with — a long-distance swap can jump one equal element over another
Insertion sortQuick sortpartition swaps elements across the whole range
Merge sortHeap sortthe heap's swaps with the last leaf reorder equal keys
Timsort, counting sortstd::sort, Arrays.sort(int[])introsort / quicksort based
Key point

Any unstable sort can be made stable by sorting (key, original index) pairs — at the cost of O(n) extra memory. And stability is irrelevant when keys are all of the data (sorting plain integers): two equal 5s are indistinguishable.

Bubble sort

Example

Input: arr = [10, 12, 5, 1, 10, 4, 56, 100]
Output: 1 4 5 10 10 12 56 100

Idea

Repeatedly walk the array and swap adjacent elements that are out of order. After pass 1 the largest element has bubbled to the end; after pass i the last i positions are final, so each pass can stop earlier. If a whole pass makes no swap the array is sorted — stop early.

Time O(n²) — O(n) best with the swapped flagSpace O(1)
  • Stable: only adjacent elements are swapped, and only when strictly greater — equal neighbours never cross.
  • In-place, trivially simple — which is why it appears in every textbook and almost no real program.
  • Without the swapped flag it always runs n − 1 full passes, even on sorted input.

Selection sort

Example

Input: arr = [29, 10, 14, 37, 13]
Output: 10 13 14 29 37

Idea

Position i should hold the i-th smallest value. Find the minimum of the unsorted part arr[i..n-1] and swap it into position i; the sorted prefix grows by one each pass. Exactly n − 1 swaps, whatever the input.

Time Θ(n²) in every caseSpace O(1)
  • Always Θ(n²) comparisons — it cannot notice that the input is already sorted.
  • Fewest memory writes of the simple sorts (at most n − 1 swaps), useful when writes are expensive (flash memory). Cycle sort is the optimum for writes.
  • Not stable: in pass 1 on [2a, 2b, 1] the 1 is swapped with 2a, which lands after 2b.
  • In-place. Its idea — repeatedly extract the minimum — is the seed of heap sort, which extracts it in O(log n) instead of O(n).

Insertion sort

Example

Input: arr = [10, 12, 5, 1, 10, 4]
Output: 1 4 5 10 10 12

Idea

Keep the prefix arr[0..i-1] sorted (as you would sort cards in your hand). Take the next element x = arr[i], shift every larger element of the prefix one slot to the right, and drop x into the gap. On nearly sorted input almost nothing shifts, which is why it is O(n) in the best case.

Time O(n²) worst / average · O(n) best (sorted input)Space O(1)
  • Stable (shifts only strictly greater elements) and in-place.
  • The practical choice for small arrays (≈ 16–32 elements) and nearly sorted data — Timsort and introsort both switch to insertion sort for short ranges.
  • O(n + d) where d is the number of inversions: an array with few elements out of place sorts in almost linear time.
Pitfall

The original notes compared x < l[i] in the inner loop. l[i] is x, so the condition is never true and nothing is ever shifted — the array came back unsorted. The comparison must be against arr[j], the element being shifted.

Merging two sorted arrays

Example

Input: a = [10, 15, 20], b = [5, 6, 6, 30]
Output: 5 6 6 10 15 20 30

Naive: concatenate and sort — O((m + n) log(m + n)). It ignores the fact that both inputs are already sorted.

Idea

Two pointers. The smallest remaining element of the union is either a[i] or b[j] — the heads of the two arrays. Compare them, copy the smaller one to the result and advance its pointer. When one array runs out, copy the rest of the other. Every element is looked at once: O(m + n).

Time O(m + n)Space O(m + n) for the result
Key point

Use <= (not <) when comparing a[i] with b[j]: on a tie the element from the left array is taken first, which is what makes merge sort stable.

Merge subarray

Example

Input: a = [10, 15, 20, 11, 13], low = 0, mid = 2, high = 4
Output: 10 11 13 15 20

Merge sort needs the same merge, but inside one array: the two sorted halves are a[low..mid] and a[mid+1..high], and the merged result must land back in a[low..high]. Copy the two halves into temporary arrays left and right, then merge them back starting at index low.

Time O(high − low + 1)Space O(high − low + 1) temporary copies

Merge sort

Example

Input: arr = [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]
Output: 3 9 10 27 38 43 82

Idea

Divide and conquer. A one-element array is sorted. Otherwise split the array in half, sort each half recursively, and merge the two sorted halves with the merge above. All the real work happens in the merges: log n levels, each merging n elements in total.

Time Θ(n log n) in every caseSpace O(n) temporary arrays + O(log n) stack
T(n) = 2 T(n / 2) + Θ(n) ⇒ T(n) = Θ(n log n)
  • Stable (the <= in merge) and guaranteed Θ(n log n) — no bad inputs, unlike quick sort.
  • Not in-place: the merge needs O(n) temporary space. (In-place variants exist but are slow or complex.)
  • Ideal for linked lists: splitting and merging lists needs no extra array, so it sorts a list in O(1) auxiliary space — and it is the default list sort in many libraries.
  • Used in external sorting (data larger than memory): sort chunks that fit in RAM, then merge the sorted chunks sequentially from disk.
  • Timsort is merge sort with insertion-sorted runs; it is what Python and Java's object sort run.
Pitfall

Writing mergeSort(a, mid, high) for the right half re-includes a[mid] in both halves and recurses forever on two elements. The halves are [low..mid] and [mid+1..high].

Union of two sorted arrays

Example

Input: a = [3, 5, 8, 9, 10, 15], b = [2, 8, 9, 10, 15]
Output: 2 3 5 8 9 10 15
Input: a = [1, 1, 3, 3, 5], b = [1, 2, 2, 3]
Output: 1 2 3 5

The union is every distinct value present in either array, in sorted order. Naive: concatenate, sort, then print each element that differs from its predecessor — O((m + n) log(m + n)).

Idea

It is the merge two-pointer walk with two extra rules: skip an element equal to the previous one in its own array (duplicates within an array), and when a[i] == b[j] output it once and advance both pointers (duplicates across the arrays). The leftovers after one array is exhausted need the same within-array duplicate check.

Time O(m + n)Space O(m + n) for the result
Pitfall

The original notes' leftover loops printed an element only when it equalled its predecessor and advanced the pointer only in that case — so they printed the wrong values and looped forever on a non-duplicate. The leftover loop must advance on every iteration and print when the element differs from its predecessor.

Intersection of two sorted arrays

Example

Input: a = [3, 5, 10, 10, 10, 10, 15, 15, 20], b = [5, 10, 10, 15, 30]
Output: 5 10 15

The intersection is every distinct value present in both arrays. Naive: for each element of a (skipping repeats), scan b for it — O(m · n).

Idea

Two pointers again. Skip duplicates in a. If a[i] < b[j], a[i] cannot be in b any more — advance i; if a[i] > b[j] advance j; if equal, output it and advance both. Duplicates in b are harmless: after a match i moves to a larger value, so the repeated b[j] is simply skipped by the > rule.

Time O(m + n)Space O(min(m, n)) for the result
Key point

Union and intersection on unsorted arrays: put one array in a hash set and scan the other — O(m + n) expected time, O(m) space. Sorting first costs O(n log n) but needs no extra memory and keeps the output sorted.

Count inversions

Inversion — a pair of indices i < j with arr[i] > arr[j] — two elements that are in the wrong order relative to each other. A sorted array has 0 inversions; a reverse-sorted one has n(n − 1) / 2. The count measures how unsorted an array is.

Example

Input: arr = [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]
Output: 3 — the pairs (2,1), (4,1), (4,3)
Input: arr = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
Output: 10

Naive: check every pair — O(n²).

Idea

Piggy-back on merge sort. Split the array at mid; every inversion (x, y) has both elements in the left half, both in the right half, or x on the left and y on the right. The first two kinds are counted by the recursive calls. The third kind is counted during the merge: when right[j] is taken before left[i], it is smaller than left[i] and every element after it in the sorted left half — that is len(left) − i inversions at once.

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)
Pitfall

Use <= when comparing left[i] with right[j]: equal elements are not an inversion (arr[i] > arr[j] is strict), so a tie must take the left element without counting. The count can reach n(n − 1) / 2 ≈ 5 × 10¹⁷ for n = 10⁹ — use a 64-bit integer in C++/Java.

Partition around a pivot

Partition — rearranging arr[low..high] around a chosen pivot value so that everything ≤ pivot comes before everything > pivot, and returning the boundary. It is the heart of quick sort: after partitioning, the pivot is in its final sorted position and the two sides can be sorted independently.

Example

Input: arr = [3, 8, 6, 12, 10, 7], pivot = arr[5] = 7
Output: 3 6 7 8 12 10 (any order inside each side is valid)

Naive, stable partition: move the pivot to the end, copy the ≤ pivot elements and then the > pivot elements into a temporary array, copy back — O(n) time but O(n) extra space.

The two in-place schemes below do it in O(1) extra space. Both are unstable.

Lomuto partition

Example

Input: arr = [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70], pivot = arr[high] = 70
Output: pivot index 4, arr = 10 30 40 50 70 90 80

Idea

Pivot is the last element. Keep an index i marking the end of the ≤ pivot zone (initially low − 1). Scan j from low to high − 1: whenever arr[j] ≤ pivot, grow the zone (i++) and swap arr[j] into it. Finally swap the pivot into position i + 1 — it is now exactly between the two zones, so it is guaranteed to be in its final place.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

Lomuto returns the pivot's final index — quick sort then recurses on [low..p−1] and [p+1..high], never touching p again. To use a different pivot (random, median-of-three), swap it to arr[high] first.

Hoare partition

Example

Input: arr = [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70, 100, 120, 10, 5], pivot = arr[low] = 10
Output: returns 1, arr = 5 10 30 90 40 50 70 100 120 80 10

Idea

Pivot is the first element. Two indices walk towards each other: i from the left stops at an element ≥ pivot, j from the right stops at one ≤ pivot. If they have not crossed, swap and continue; once i ≥ j, return j. Everything in [low..j] is ≤ pivot and everything in [j+1..high] is ≥ pivot — but the pivot itself can be anywhere in the left part, so quick sort must recurse on [low..j] and [j+1..high], not skip j.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
LomutoHoare
Pivotlast element arr[high]first element arr[low]
Returnsthe pivot's final index pa boundary j; the pivot is somewhere in [low..j]
Quick sort recursion[low..p−1] and [p+1..high][low..j] and [j+1..high]
Swapsabout n/2 on averageabout n/6 — roughly three times fewer
All-equal inputdegenerates: every element goes left → O(n²)splits in the middle → stays O(n log n)
Simplicityeasier to get rightthe stop conditions and the i >= j test are easy to get wrong
Pitfall

With Hoare, recursing on [low..j−1] and [j+1..high] (as for Lomuto) loses the element at j, which is not necessarily the pivot. And the inner loops must use strict < / > — with <= they can run off the ends of the array.

Quick sort

Example

Input: arr = [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70]
Output: 10 30 40 50 70 80 90
Input: arr = [3, 5, 6, 7, 1, 2, 4]
Output: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7

Idea

Divide and conquer where the work is in the divide: partition the array around a pivot, then sort the two sides recursively. There is no merge step — once both sides are sorted, the whole array is, because every left element ≤ pivot ≤ every right element.

Time O(n log n) average · O(n²) worstSpace O(log n) stack on average

Analysis of quick sort

CaseWhenRecurrenceTime
Bestevery partition splits in halfT(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n)Θ(n log n)
Averagerandom pivots / random inputT(n) = T(n/4) + T(3n/4) + Θ(n) (a typical uneven split)Θ(n log n) — about 1.39 n log2 n comparisons
Worstthe pivot is always the min or max — sorted input with first/last pivot, or all equal values with LomutoT(n) = T(n − 1) + Θ(n)Θ(n²)
Spacerecursion depthO(log n) average; O(n) in the worst case unless the smaller side is recursed first

Despite the O(n²) worst case, quick sort is usually the fastest comparison sort in practice:

In-place

Partition needs O(1) extra memory; merge sort needs an O(n) buffer.

Cache-friendly

Partition sweeps the array sequentially; heap sort jumps around and misses the cache.

Small constants

The inner loop is a compare and an occasional swap — less work per element than merge sort's copying.

Tail recursion

The second recursive call can become a loop; recursing on the smaller side first bounds the stack at O(log n).

Worst case is avoidable

A random pivot (or median-of-three) makes the O(n²) case astronomically unlikely; introsort falls back to heap sort if the depth gets too large.

Not stable

Both in-place partitions move elements across the range, so equal keys can swap order. Use merge sort / Timsort when stability matters.

Pitfall

Three statements in the original notes were wrong: the best case is Θ(n log n), not Θ(log n) — you cannot sort without looking at every element; the space complexity is O(log n) on average (recursion depth), not Θ(n); and Hoare's partition is not "three times faster" overall — it does about three times fewer swaps on average, which makes it somewhat faster. Hoare also handles many equal keys gracefully, while Lomuto degrades to O(n²) on them.

Key point

std::sort in C++ is introsort: quick sort with median-of-three pivots, switching to heap sort when the recursion depth exceeds 2 log n and to insertion sort for ranges of ≈ 16 elements. Java sorts primitives with a dual-pivot quick sort. Both are O(n log n) worst case in practice.

Heap sort

Example

Input: arr = [4, 10, 3, 5, 1, 12, 7]
Output: 1 3 4 5 7 10 12

Idea

Selection sort finds the maximum in O(n) per pass; a max-heap finds it in O(1) and restores itself in O(log n). So: build a max-heap from the array in place, then repeatedly swap the root (the maximum) with the last element of the heap, shrink the heap by one and heapify the new root down. The sorted elements accumulate at the end of the array.

1
heapify(i)
Compare node i with its children; swap with the larger child if it is bigger, and continue down. O(log n).
2
build heap
Call heapify on every internal node from the last one (n/2 − 1) down to the root. Leaves are already heaps. This takes O(n) in total, not O(n log n).
3
extract
For i = n − 1 … 1: swap arr[0] (the max) with arr[i], then heapify(0) on the heap of size i. Each extraction is O(log n).
Time O(n log n) in every caseSpace O(1)
  • An optimisation of selection sort: the same extract the extreme, shrink the range loop, with an O(log n) extraction instead of O(n).
  • Guaranteed O(n log n) and in-place — the combination merge sort and quick sort each lack. The price: poor cache locality, so it is slower than quick sort in practice.
  • Not stable: swapping the root with the last leaf can jump an element over equal keys.
  • Used as the fallback inside introsort (std::sort) and wherever a worst-case guarantee matters. The heap itself is the DSA Basics → Heap topic.

Interview Q&A

Which sorting algorithm would you pick, and why?

For general use, the library sort: Timsort (Python/Java objects/JS) or introsort (std::sort). Hand-rolled: quick sort for speed on arrays in memory; merge sort when stability or a guaranteed n log n is needed, for linked lists, or for data that does not fit in memory; heap sort when memory is tight and the worst case must be bounded; insertion sort for tiny or nearly sorted inputs; counting/radix sort when keys are small integers.

What does stable mean, and which algorithms are stable?

Equal keys keep their input order. Stable: bubble, insertion, merge, Timsort, counting sort. Not stable: selection, quick, heap, std::sort. It matters for multi-key sorts (sort by name, then stably by marks) and for sorting records by one field while keeping a meaningful prior order.

Why is quick sort faster than merge sort in practice if both are O(n log n)?

Quick sort partitions in place with a tight inner loop and sequential memory access; merge sort copies every element into a buffer at every level. Quick sort does more comparisons on average (≈ 1.39 n log n vs n log n) but fewer memory moves and far fewer cache misses. Merge sort wins on linked lists, on stability, and when a worst-case guarantee is required.

When does quick sort degrade to O(n²), and how do you prevent it?

When every partition is maximally unbalanced: already sorted or reverse-sorted input with a first/last pivot, or many equal keys with Lomuto. Fixes: choose a random pivot or the median of three, use Hoare or three-way (Dutch flag) partitioning for duplicates, recurse on the smaller side first to cap the stack, and switch to heap sort if the depth exceeds 2 log n (introsort).

Can you sort in better than O(n log n)?

Not by comparing: a comparison sort must distinguish n! permutations, which needs log2(n!) = Θ(n log n) comparisons. Non-comparison sorts use the structure of the keys: counting sort is O(n + k) for integers in 0..k, radix sort O(d(n + k)) for d-digit keys, bucket sort for uniformly distributed reals.

What is the difference between sort() and sorted() in Python?

list.sort() sorts the list in place and returns None; sorted(iterable) accepts any iterable and returns a new list, leaving the input untouched. Both are Timsort, stable, and take the same key= and reverse= arguments.

Why does [10, 9, 1].sort() give [1, 10, 9] in JavaScript?

Without a comparator, Array.prototype.sort converts elements to strings and compares them lexicographically: "10" < "9" because "1" < "9". Always pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.

How many swaps does selection sort make, and why is that interesting?

At most n − 1 — one per pass — regardless of input, versus O(n²) for bubble sort and O(n²) shifts for insertion sort. On media where writes are expensive (flash) that can matter; cycle sort takes the idea to its limit with the minimum possible number of writes.
